fields.hint: Context is not free: every consumer re-renders when the Provider's value changes, memo or not. Ask what it was designed to remove instead.
fields.explanation: Context removes the chore of threading a prop through components that never use it: the value goes in at a Provider and any descendant reads it directly. It is not a render optimization, since every consumer re-renders when the Provider's value changes, even one wrapped in memo. The value still lives in ordinary state somewhere, so it disappears when that owner unmounts.

fields.hint: Some components between the Provider and a consumer never read this context. Decide whether React has any reason to update those.
fields.explanation: Reading a context subscribes the component, so when the Provider's value changes every consumer below re-renders, including one wrapped in React.memo, because the update arrives through the context rather than through props. A component that reads nothing from the context gets no update from the context itself, though it still re-renders if its own parent does. This is also why passing a fresh object literal as the value re-renders all consumers on every parent render, and why that value is worth memoizing when the tree is large.

Index keys are safe only when the list never reorders and items are only ever added or removed at the end.

fields.explanation: memo keeps the previous props and compares them value by value with Object.is, so when the parent re-renders and every prop is the same value React reuses the previous output. It does nothing about renders that start inside the component: its own state update, and a change in a context it reads, re-render it either way. A prop that is a new object with the same contents counts as changed, because the comparison is shallow, and even with equal props React may still re-render: memo is an optimization, not a guarantee.

fields.explanation: useCallback caches the function and returns the identical object until a dependency changes, so the memoized child sees the same onClick prop and skips its re-render. useEffect returns nothing you could pass down, and useState hands back a setter that is stable but is not the handler you wrote. Without useCallback the inline handler is a new object each render and memo compares it as changed.

fields.explanation: An empty dependency array tells React there is nothing to watch, so the body runs after the first render and never again: one request goes out and setItems puts the JSON into state.
